lines.text: Does electric current get used up?
You've been told it does. It doesn't, and two meters can prove it.
Most of us picture the same thing. Current leaves the battery full, the bulb drinks some, and only a little makes it back.
It sounds logical. It's wrong. Put one meter right before the bulb, and another right after.
They read exactly the same. Half an amp in, half an amp out. Not a single electron is lost along the way.
So what gets used up? Energy. Electrons go in pushed hard, and come out tired.
Same electrons, less energy. What drops is the voltage, not the current.
This has a name: Kirchhoff's current law. Wherever wires meet, everything that goes in has to come out.
If three amps arrive and the circuit splits in two, two go one way and one goes the other.
Three in, three out. Like a roundabout: no car disappears.
Current isn't used up. It's shared. What gets used up is energy.
